paragraphs.text: A [raw pu’er](sheng:identity) cake made in 1996 from leaf grown in Menghai County, Yunnan. [Menghai](menghai-county:county-and-factory) on a label can mean the county or the factory that stands in it. This record names the county as the leaf’s origin and says nothing of a maker.
Thirty years on, it is past the point where the trade says [raw pu’er counts as aged](sheng:ageing). Some put that point at ten years, and many wait for twenty or more.

Unlike shou, it was never put through a fast fermentation, so it has [changed slowly](sheng:aging) in [storage](sheng:storage). Oxidation and microbes do that work, which is why warmth and humidity set how fast a tea changes. [Pressing](sheng:pressing) began so tea would travel well on the old trade routes. It also shapes ageing, since a tight cake changes more slowly than a loose one.

brewing.text: Pry the leaf off a cake or brick in chunks with a pick or knife, from the surface and toward the centre, rather than crumbling it. A mix of larger pieces and smaller ones brews evenly. Young raw pu’er takes water a little off the boil, about 85 to 95°C, because hotter water draws out more of its bitterness; an aged one takes 95°C to boiling. A common start is about 7 grams to 100 ml and a quick rinse of a few seconds, then a first steep of ten to fifteen seconds, adding a few seconds each round. A good raw tea gives eight to ten cups or more.

notice.text: A smoother, thicker, sweeter cup with woody, herbal and camphor notes and something of dried dates or dark fruit.
